documents: Grande, Zimmer & Mallard (2022), Hydrological Processes 36:e14697, published paper (PDF, 17 pages)

entry.evidence: The intra-annual variability in P partitioning may not explain the differentiation between water- and energy-limited catchments

steps.action: Named the gap that intra-annual storage dynamics and S-Q relationships across the water/energy-limitation spectrum, especially near the threshold, are poorly understood, and asked when energy-limited catchments behave like water-limited ones and the reverse.
steps.quote: However, the dynamics of S at intra-annual time scales (e.g., aggregated precipitation events or monthly aggregates) remain poorly understood in many hydroclimates.

steps.action: Selected two threshold catchments (Calhoun, Tilden) and two strongly energy-limited ones (Lower Hafren, Luquillo), with one 'Normal' and one 'Wet' water year per site chosen to match precipitation percentiles across sites.
steps.quote: Thus, we chose data from Lower Hafren (1992 water year and 2007 water year in the 40th and 92nd percentile, respectively)

steps.action: Used daily P, Q and ET records for Calhoun (weir, tipping bucket, Thornthwaite PET with AET taken as equal to PET) and Tilden (CDEC P, EBRPD stage and rating curve, satellite CalETa AET, irrigation added to P), collected in the authors' earlier work.
steps.quote: The data from Calhoun were collected and maintained as described in (Mallard, 2020).

steps.action: Took public daily hydroclimatic data for Lower Hafren (Harman 2015, Penman-Monteith-based AET) and Luquillo (Silver & Leon 2019; Zimmerman 2018), and computed Thornthwaite PET for Luquillo.
steps.quote: publicly available hydroclimatic data from Lower Hafren and Luquillo

steps.action: Estimated daily relative catchment storage as the cumulative P - Q - ET from 1 October with S0 = 0, assuming minimum storage at the start of the water year, and computed antecedent and per-event storage.
steps.quote: Relative storage (mm) for each day (t) was estimated as:

steps.action: Defined an inclusive P-and-Q event delineation rule (301 events), computed event runoff ratios with recession-based baseflow separation (EcoHydRology), and normalized event totals by event length.
steps.quote: we defined precipitation events from the onset of P ≥ 1 mm/day to when Q had receded to 120% of pre-event

steps.action: Reported annual water budgets, runoff ratios and ET/P for each site and year (Table 1), including Tilden switching from water-limited to energy-limited between the normal and wet years.
steps.quote: we found a shift between water-limited in the normal water year and energy-limited in the wet water year at Tilden

steps.action: Described event-scale seasonal partitioning at each site: storage-dominated partitioning early in the water year, runoff-dominated partitioning in winter and spring, and ET-dominated partitioning in summer (Figures 3, 4; Table 2).
steps.quote: In both water years from Calhoun, the event RRs increased from the onset of the water year and then decreased in mid-to-late spring

steps.action: Established a recurring pattern in the storage time series across years and sites and categorized it into wet-up, plateau and dry-down stages.
steps.quote: Based on this common pattern in S across water years and sites, we categorized S seasonality into three different stages

steps.action: Checked that clockwise S-RR hysteresis recurs in both threshold catchments and in each of the two water years at each of them (Figure 5).
steps.quote: the S-RR relationship revealed hysteretic behaviour with a clockwise direction across each water year

steps.action: Compared the S-RR behaviour of the threshold catchments with the strongly energy-limited reference catchments, which show no hysteresis and little storage variability.
steps.quote: In contrast, hysteretic behaviour was not observed in the S-RR relationship for the strongly energy-limited watersheds

steps.action: Retained the claim that catchment storage drives event runoff ratios across the studied hydroclimates.
steps.quote: Across the hydroclimatic spectrum considered in our study, event RRs exhibited a strong relationship with S

steps.action: Restricted the range of the claim to catchments dominated by saturation-excess or subsurface flow, excluding Hortonian, high-intensity rainfall systems such as arid or urban catchments.
steps.quote: In catchments dominated by Hortonian Overland Flow and high-intensity rainfall events

steps.action: Set the result against earlier studies on watershed memory and seasonal partitioning (Nippgen 2016, Yokoo 2008, Wang 2011).
steps.quote: The work presented in the literature and our results highlight the role of watershed S in moderating P partitioning

steps.action: Proposed a conceptual model of three storage stages (Figure 6), with the plateau tied to a catchment storage threshold and dry-down controlled by ET or by P-ET asynchrony depending on hydroclimate.
steps.quote: we divided S into three dominant stages across a given water year: wet-up, plateau, and dry-down

steps.action: Compared the stage framework with fill-and-spill threshold studies and with the Fovet et al. (2015) and Spence et al. (2010) S-Q periods, noting that Fovet omitted ET.
steps.quote: This conceptual framework for categorizing S behaviour in catchments is consistent with other studies.

steps.action: Hypothesized, after Dralle et al. (2018), that ET redistributes dry-down precipitation into indirect, plant-accessible storage, which would explain the higher RR in wet-up than in dry-down at equal storage.
steps.quote: We hypothesize redistribution of the incoming P during the dry-down stage into less hydraulically active but more plant-accessible storage zones

steps.action: Concluded that the shared storage-stage behaviour of the two threshold catchments indicates a characteristic behaviour of catchments near the water/energy threshold, and proposed the framework for cross-catchment comparison.
steps.quote: suggests a characteristic behaviour of catchments close to this threshold

end.claim: Catchments near the water/energy-limitation threshold pass through wet-up, plateau and dry-down storage stages, with clockwise S-RR hysteresis (higher RR in wet-up than in dry-down at equal storage) that is absent in strongly energy-limited catchments; the claim is limited to catchments not dominated by Hortonian flow.

decisive_move.sentence: Estimating daily relative storage as the cumulative water-balance residual made the storage stages and the S-RR hysteresis visible; without it there are no stages to compare.

gates.evidence: Catchments were chosen because they were 'expected to have the highest dependence on storage' (p. 9), but the data were collected earlier for other purposes or taken from public archives. The threshold-versus-energy-limited contrast in hysteresis could have failed, but the stage categorization is descriptive and was drawn after inspecting the data (p. 8). Nothing was fixed before the data were seen.

Hysteresis as a descriptor of storage-runoff loops

novelty_claims.quote: We believe our work can serve as a first assessment for periods
The conceptual model of storage stages in the present study thus advances ideas proposed by Fovet et al. (2015) and Spence et al. (2010)
However, here we use a direct estimation of storage.

limits: No review file was supplied, so no review sequence is coded, although the acknowledgements credit the editor and two reviewers with improvements. The authors acknowledge that only two water years per site were analysed (p. 12-13). The paper argues, but does not test, that ET magnitude errors would only shift the storage curve (p. 13); no sensitivity run is reported. Other untested premises: S0 = 0 on 1 October, AET taken as equal to PET at energy-limited sites, and the irrigation lumping. The event threshold (1 mm/d, 120%) was not varied. Inference: the stage categorization appears to have been drawn after seeing the storage curves, not fixed in advance. Sub-claims at other statuses: the ET-driven redistribution into indirect storage (p. 12) is a proposed hypothesis with status none; transferability across hydroclimates (p. 10) is asserted from four catchments, closer to best_explanation; the management implications (p. 13-14) are untested. There are internal inconsistencies: the Tilden wet/normal years are labelled 2018/2017 on p. 7 against 2017/2018 in Table 1; Tilden wet-year ET is 782 mm in the text (p. 6) against 1049 mm in Table 1; and the Calhoun year labels are swapped on p. 7. Data are available only on request.

disagreements.target: Fovet et al. (2015), hysteresis periods of the S-Q relationship
disagreements.support: The paper's dry-down stage and its wet-up versus dry-down RR difference are attributed to ET, which Fovet et al. left out of their periods.
disagreements.quote: Interestingly, Fovet et al. (2015) did not consider the role of ET in their characterization of the different periods.

disagreements.target: Annual water balance / Budyko-space classification of catchments as water- or energy-limited
disagreements.support: Event and monthly partitioning shows threshold catchments switching between water- and energy-limited behaviour within a year, which annual averages mask.
disagreements.quote: However, annual water balance studies may 'miss' the intra-annual variability in runoff generation

disagreements.target: Previous studies using storage proxies (antecedent precipitation indices, water table measurements)
disagreements.support: The paper uses a water-balance estimate of integrated storage instead, conceding a tradeoff in uncertainty.
disagreements.quote: Previous studies have used other proxies for storage, such as antecedent precipitation indices, or water table measurements.

alternatives_considered.chosen: Events from onset of P ≥ 1 mm/day until Q recedes to 120% of pre-event flow or a new event starts
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Rainfall-only definitions (Singh et al. 2018; Rinderer et al. 2016); Q thresholds (Rose & Peters 2001); groundwater thresholds (Meerveld et al. 2015); baseflow separation (Blume et al. 2007; Merz et al. 2006); start of P to end of quickflow (Detty & McGuire 2010; McCarter et al. 2020)
alternatives_considered.reason: Precipitation regimes vary across catchments and the approach must extract periods across the entire water year

alternatives_considered.chosen: Recession-analysis baseflow separation (Sujono et al. 2004) in the EcoHydRology R package
alternatives_considered.reason: Simplicity, and successful prior use on daily streamflow series

alternatives_considered.chosen: Direct water-balance estimate of relative storage
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Storage proxies such as antecedent precipitation indices or water table measurements
alternatives_considered.reason: Direct estimation of integrated storage, at the cost of uncertainty

alternatives_considered.chosen: Two water years per catchment matched on precipitation percentiles
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Longer records available at Lower Hafren and Luquillo
alternatives_considered.reason: Data availability at Calhoun and Tilden; comparability of precipitation percentiles

alternatives_considered.chosen: Irrigation water combined with P as a single input at Tilden
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Treating irrigation as a separate water budget component (implied)
alternatives_considered.reason: Irrigation is applied in a small area and is less than 3% of P over the period
